RIAH PHIYEGA

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we speak to insiders about the legacy National Commissioner Riah Phiyega has left on the police

Summary:
Phiyega's last days - we hear first hand what really went down inside the police from a highly placed police source.



Further information:
CITIZEN ARTICLE
South Africa’s nine provincial police commissioners have come out strongly in support of under fire National Commissioner Riah Phiyega, saying they are concerned about the “unfair and negative” attitude towards her.

The Board of Commissioners of the South African Police Service (SAPS), a structure representing the nine provincial commissioners, issued a statement on Saturday night in which it declared its full support for their boss. The Farlam Commission of Inquiry, set up to investigate the 2012 Marikana massacre in North West, recommended in its report released last month that the national commissioner face an inquiry into her fitness to hold office.

Phiyega was given until Friday to submit her reasons in writing to President Jacob Zuma as to why she should not face an inquiry. She filed her response at around 11pm on Friday. On Saturday, the Board of Commissioners said it “is concerned about the prevailing unfair and largely negative attitude towards the National Commissioner of the SAPS, General Riah Phiyega”.

“The board has noticed a tendency to reduce everything, especially negative issues relating to policing, to the person of the National Commissioner, as if the SAPS is a one-person show.”

The statement added: It is therefore appropriate that the board publicly declares its full support for General Phiyega, and fully endorses her efforts in turning around the SAPS. We are compelled to take this stance as some unnamed sources are misinforming the media, alleging that we are unhappy with the National Commissioner.”

It said media reports claiming low morale, breaking of ranks, and an overall messy state of affairs within the SAPS were unfounded.

“As the SAPS top management, working closely with General Phiyega, we are surprised by these reports, as at no stage has our morale been low. As the nine provincial commissioners we are committed in executing our work together with our members and we shall continue doing so unabated.”

The board further mentioned that it should be noted that none of the SAPS management structures had taken a resolution not to support the submission made at the Farlam Commission of Inquiry.

“It is not true that the current management is prioritising task teams over the detectives. The fact of the matter is that these cross-functional teams that we set up have proved very successful. It must be placed on record that the detectives at police stations, as well as at relevant specialised units, continue to execute their duties as usual and remarkable successes have been secured.

“The cases involving [Radovan] Krejcir, [Christopher] Panayiotou, mall robberies, truck hijackings, gangsterism, and drugs are all dealt with by multi-disciplinary teams. The task team dealing with robbers targeting vehicles transporting cigarettes has made significant progress and the same can be said about the so-called airport-following cases.

“Statistics in this regard speak for themselves. At the centre of the successes is the closer working relationship between the detectives and crime intelligence, which is allegedly dysfunctional if one is to believe reports.”

The board said that when the National Commissioner joined the SAPS, the Crime Intelligence Division was in the “Intensive Care Unit, with many issues being exposed in the media”.

“The division is now out of the ICU and results are starting to show. Leadership has stabilised following the appointment of 26 skilled and experienced managers to effectively drive the envisaged turnaround strategy in support of the SAPS objectives. By the end April next year, we would have appointed an additional 900 officers.”

In a lengthy statement, the SAPS board pointed to successes achieved due to the work of the Crime Intelligence Division, saying that targets for 2014/15 which were presented to parliament’s police portfolio committee, including the conducting of 32,507 operations and the generation of 261,193 intelligence products to address priority crimes, were on line to be exceeded.

The board also said the detective services had been working on ways and means of improving the conviction rate, tracing wanted suspects, and improving command and control for better service delivery.

“Under the current management there has been a great deal of focus on strategy, so as to get the fundamentals right, because if [the] SAPS is to fight crime effectively in a sustainable manner, it must be administratively sound. This is informed by the fact that crime is an evolving phenomenon. Policing should therefore be dynamic in order to respond appropriately.”

To meet the challenges the SAPS management said it was:

– Promoting integrity by vetting all senior management, including lifestyle and skills audits to assist in managing corruption within the police;
– Professionalising the police through amendments to standing orders and establishing the SAPS University in Paarl, as well as by engaging various tertiary institutions to come up with courses and programmes which would strengthen the leadership of the SAPS;
– Signing a number of memoranda of understanding with various stakeholders such as Statistics South Africa, Business Against Crime, the CSIR, SABRIC, Primedia/Crime Line, the SABC, and the SA Human Rights Commission in order to improve the quality of policing in the country; and
– Establishing National Disciplinary Trial Units to ensure speedy, standardised, and consistent handling of disciplinary issues to effectively deal with issues of negative discipline and violations of the SAPS Code of Conduct.

“All the nine provincial commissioners wish to state categorically that they are committed to the fight against crime, and continue to motivate their members,” the statement added.

“The successes of Operation Fiela, a countrywide operation aimed at targeting places where the criminal element has manifested itself, speaks volumes regarding [the] SAPS’s commitment to fighting crime.

“This statement of the Board of Commissioners is fully supported by the Deputy National Commissioner: Corporate Services – Lieutenant-General Nobubele Mbekela, the Deputy National Commissioner: Policing – Lieutenant-General Kehla Sitole, and acting Divisional Commissioner Lieutenant-General Bongiwe Zulu.

“Each and every individual provincial commissioner is fully behind this media statement and may be contacted by media representatives directly to verify this fact.”

Press Release:


Riah Phiyega
Police commissioner Riah Phiyega could face the axe, following recommendations in reports on Marikana that she should be charged, or face remedial action. But Phiyega is standing strong and it’s believed she has already asked Zuma for a second chance after submitting her response to him. Nine Provincial Commissioners have openly pledged their support for her, but insiders reveal a serious lack of respect from senior police members she leads. Carte Blanche asks whether a political appointee can ever be fit to hold office as National Police Commissioner?


Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: THE STATISTICS DON’T LIE… CRIME IS UP!

There are more armed robberies (11.2%), more hijackings (12.3%) and more people murdered (47 a day)….All under National Police Commissoner Riah Piyega’s watch, since she took over in 2012.

IS POLICE LEADERSHIP TO BLAME?

INSIDER 1: This is not Transnet or ABSA, the mistakes we make are paid for in blood.
VO: THIS high-ranking career policeman, who didn’t want his identity revealed is referring to our top cop’s corporate background. He doesn’t believe she’s equipped for the job she’s been trying to do for the past 3 years.

First there was the Marikana Massacre - just two months in to the job.

UP SOUND: RIAH PHIYEGA
RIAH: AS A LEADER I HAD TO COME IN AND says lets Remember all we can do is show how we policed, all we can do is tell the truth ..”

VO: The Farlam Commission into the Marikana Massacre found that Riah Phiyega lacked integrity and was dishonest.

INSIDER: she appeared to try to justify the police’s actions, and now she is adjusting her stance by blaming her subordinates. If you are the National Commissioner you walk in front, you take the decisions, if there is a balls up, the buck stops with you.

VO: She now has to explain herself to the President.

DEVI: Why did RIAH PHIYEGA not just resign?
SOLOMON: Your understanding is that there is trouble and that national commissioner should run away. The national commissioner wants to account – as she has been asked to – I don’t think running away is the solution.

VO: Representing the National Commissioner, Police Spokesperson Solomon Makgale says responding to the President is not unusual – it’s simply procedure.

LAST WEEK, The SAPS Board of Commissioners, representing the police in all 9 provinces, released a lengthy statement defending Riah Phiyega.

UPSOUND: 702 AUDIO CLIP:
Lt Gen Nobubele Makhabela: It was a statement to dispel the myth and all the rumours running around indicating that the national commissioner has no support on the side of the police, // we support the national commissioner. // We won’t waver in that.

VO: It feels like history could be repeating it self. When former National Police Commissoner, Jacki Selebi was accused of corruption police top brass rallied round him.

JOHAN: // we know how that ended – he was sentenced to jail for 15 years, in spite of all the support that he received

VO: Former SAPS Major-General, now Senior Researcher at the Institute for Security Studies dr. Johan Burger, says the FARLAM findings should be taken seriously by the Board of commissioners.

DEVI: What does it say about our provincial commissioners?
JOHAN: poor reflection – no one wants to be singled out even though she stands being accused of being dishonest, lying.

VO: The statement has landed them in hot water – next week all 9 provincial commissioners will have to answer in parliament why they strayed from their task of fighting crime to politics.

LINK: The unions are not united and some are not holding back – they’re more vocal in their criticism than others.

VO: It is time for change – AGAIN - says SAPS UNION President Mpho Mwanika. The union represents around 80 000 policemen. He believes it’s time for Riah Phiyega to hang up your uniform and take off her medals.

DEVI: Should she get a second chance?
MPHO: NO! //She is the accounting officer, who must we blame is things goes wrong in depart, must we go look for the minister of Corrections Services to take the blame for her department.

INSIDER 1: She is too arrogant to realize her own shortcomings – that is her problem. // Since her appointment crime has spiraled out of control because she disrupted proven management systems that were working.

VO: A sentiment echoed by a senior detective with over 20 years experience fighting crime – he too asked that we protect his identity.

INSIDER 2: The morale is down down down. You can see why there is so much crime they are focusing on not fighting crime.

SOLOMON No one is going to say to acceptable that crime is high, it is not acceptable, she herself has said that. Stories about the morale being down, stories about mutiny, stories about demotion, stories about the NC sidelining people – they are coming from sources we do not know.

VO: They may be unknown sources, but these policemen say they represent the ordinary cops who have the skills and experience to tackle crime, but they lack a key element – leadership.

LINK: The last two years has shown that nobody’s under police commissioner Riah Phiyega is secure, if you don’t tow the line, you could be shuffled around, demoted or even shown the door.

INSIDER 1: One of her biggest mistakes, is that she discarded high ranking officers. It almost appears as if she was in a self-destruct mode.

VO: Johan Burger says some of Phiyega’s decisions make no sense – like the constructive dismissal of Lt General Godfrey Lebeya and Lt Gen Leah Mofome – both held top jobs and were offered relegated positions

JOHAN: Both of them more than 30 years experience in the police. both of them doctorates, why did she go on protect Richard Mduli from both criminal prosecutiron and disciplinary action.

VO: Some policemen say she’s more concerned with politics than crime fighting.

INSIDER 2: She doesn’t know anything about police work – she has not got directions – all the seniors police officers, learned people who were kicked out of the service because of her

VO: But the official stance IS quite different – Solomon says they have nothing to fear.

SOLOMON: I am very proud to be under the leadership of the current national commissioner of the police service, I have never come across somebody that is so dedicated, somebody as hardworking….

VO: But not everyone serving under her agrees.

INSIDER 1: The mistake she makes is thinking that she is respected when people jump and salute her and say yes sir, sir no, three bags full sir, but that isn’t respect.

VO: Speaking on TALK RADIO 702, Board of Commissioners representative Lt Gen Mbekela raised the gender issue.

UPSOUND 702 CLIP
Lt Gen Mbekela: It is interesting to have noted that actually the people who have been on the attack all the time are mostly men. // this is an attack on woman leadership.

DEVI: Does Riah Phiyega feel that she’s been given a tough time because she is a woman?
SOLOMON: the south African police service is a very male dominated organization – there are people finding it very difficult to accept woman leadership – inside and outside of the organization.

INSIDER 2 NO, No, not because she is a woman, because of her attitude

JOHAN: I mean the same arguments went against Jackie Selebi – they also came from outside of the police. completely incidental that she is a woman

VO: Also from the corporate world, Lt Gen Makgale says the upper echelons of the police aren’t about crime fighting and despite her lack of police experience, the challenges are not that much different to running a commercial enterprise.

SOLOMON: Once you get into management level you run budgets and strategies, it’s no different from whether you are pick n pay, Checkers or you run a media house.

VO: But police analyst Burger, says fighting crime requires very specific skills which need to come from the top. It worked in New York City under police Chief Bill Bratton when he was appointed by Mayor Rudi Guilliani to rid corruption.

JOHAN: He didn’t go in search of a social worker or a banker, he went in search of an experienced police officer // we all know the success – today NYC has one of the most professional policing.

VO: Like many policemen having worked his way up the ranks, our insider says the National Commissioner’s biggest mistake was thinking she could do the job.

INSIDER 1: If I am asked to takeover ABSA bank tomorrow, I will most definitely decline the opportunity because I will be setting myself up for failure. She accepted the responsibility of being the national commissioner at the time, coupled with a nice salary package – but she was never qualified.

VO: The President needs to account to the people, says Johan Burger.

JOHAN: Why did he take her, who is the most unsuited person one could think of given that there is a pool of other candidates that would probably have been a better choice.

DEVI: Were you surprised that she didn’t resgin immediately?
MPHO: everywhere she is coming from she put up a fight, we expected – the president will do honourable
INSIDER 1: Career police officers who have dedicated their lives to the police will be relieved to see her go, her legacy will be a broken police service.


PROMO 1 – 15 seconds

VO: With yet another National Police Commissioner in hot water – We ask who is to blame Phiyega or the President who appointed her?

JOHAN: Why did he take her, the most unsuited person one could think of given that there is a pool of other candidates

PROMO 2 – 15 seconds
VO: Following the Marikana Report, National Commissioner Riah Phiyega now has to answer to the President.

INSIDER 1: This is not Transnet or ABSA, the mistakes we make are paid for in blood.

VO: We speak to high ranking insiders about the struggles within the police.

PROMO 3 – 10 seconds

INSIDER 1: She discarded high ranking officers. It almost appears as if she was in a self-destruct mode.

VO: Is Top Cop Riah Phiyega fit to hold office?

metadata.Summary: Phiyega's last days - we hear first hand what really went down inside the police from a highly placed police source.
metadata.Further information: CITIZEN ARTICLE South Africa’s nine provincial police commissioners have come out strongly in support of under fire National Commissioner Riah Phiyega, saying they are concerned about the “unfair and negative” attitude towards her. The Board of Commissioners of the South African Police Service (SAPS), a structure representing the nine provincial commissioners, issued a statement on Saturday night in which it declared its full support for their boss. The Farlam Commission of Inquiry, set up to investigate the 2012 Marikana massacre in North West, recommended in its report released last month that the national commissioner face an inquiry into her fitness to hold office. Phiyega was given until Friday to submit her reasons in writing to President Jacob Zuma as to why she should not face an inquiry. She filed her response at around 11pm on Friday. On Saturday, the Board of Commissioners said it “is concerned about the prevailing unfair and largely negative attitude towards the National Commissioner of the SAPS, General Riah Phiyega”. “The board has noticed a tendency to reduce everything, especially negative issues relating to policing, to the person of the National Commissioner, as if the SAPS is a one-person show.” The statement added: It is therefore appropriate that the board publicly declares its full support for General Phiyega, and fully endorses her efforts in turning around the SAPS. We are compelled to take this stance as some unnamed sources are misinforming the media, alleging that we are unhappy with the National Commissioner.” It said media reports claiming low morale, breaking of ranks, and an overall messy state of affairs within the SAPS were unfounded. “As the SAPS top management, working closely with General Phiyega, we are surprised by these reports, as at no stage has our morale been low. As the nine provincial commissioners we are committed in executing our work together with our members and we shall continue doing so unabated.” The board further mentioned that it should be noted that none of the SAPS management structures had taken a resolution not to support the submission made at the Farlam Commission of Inquiry. “It is not true that the current management is prioritising task teams over the detectives. The fact of the matter is that these cross-functional teams that we set up have proved very successful. It must be placed on record that the detectives at police stations, as well as at relevant specialised units, continue to execute their duties as usual and remarkable successes have been secured. “The cases involving [Radovan] Krejcir, [Christopher] Panayiotou, mall robberies, truck hijackings, gangsterism, and drugs are all dealt with by multi-disciplinary teams. The task team dealing with robbers targeting vehicles transporting cigarettes has made significant progress and the same can be said about the so-called airport-following cases. “Statistics in this regard speak for themselves. At the centre of the successes is the closer working relationship between the detectives and crime intelligence, which is allegedly dysfunctional if one is to believe reports.” The board said that when the National Commissioner joined the SAPS, the Crime Intelligence Division was in the “Intensive Care Unit, with many issues being exposed in the media”. “The division is now out of the ICU and results are starting to show. Leadership has stabilised following the appointment of 26 skilled and experienced managers to effectively drive the envisaged turnaround strategy in support of the SAPS objectives. By the end April next year, we would have appointed an additional 900 officers.” In a lengthy statement, the SAPS board pointed to successes achieved due to the work of the Crime Intelligence Division, saying that targets for 2014/15 which were presented to parliament’s police portfolio committee, including the conducting of 32,507 operations and the generation of 261,193 intelligence products to address priority crimes, were on line to be exceeded. The board also said the detective services had been working on ways and means of improving the conviction rate, tracing wanted suspects, and improving command and control for better service delivery. “Under the current management there has been a great deal of focus on strategy, so as to get the fundamentals right, because if [the] SAPS is to fight crime effectively in a sustainable manner, it must be administratively sound. This is informed by the fact that crime is an evolving phenomenon. Policing should therefore be dynamic in order to respond appropriately.” To meet the challenges the SAPS management said it was: – Promoting integrity by vetting all senior management, including lifestyle and skills audits to assist in managing corruption within the police; – Professionalising the police through amendments to standing orders and establishing the SAPS University in Paarl, as well as by engaging various tertiary institutions to come up with courses and programmes which would strengthen the leadership of the SAPS; – Signing a number of memoranda of understanding with various stakeholders such as Statistics South Africa, Business Against Crime, the CSIR, SABRIC, Primedia/Crime Line, the SABC, and the SA Human Rights Commission in order to improve the quality of policing in the country; and – Establishing National Disciplinary Trial Units to ensure speedy, standardised, and consistent handling of disciplinary issues to effectively deal with issues of negative discipline and violations of the SAPS Code of Conduct. “All the nine provincial commissioners wish to state categorically that they are committed to the fight against crime, and continue to motivate their members,” the statement added. “The successes of Operation Fiela, a countrywide operation aimed at targeting places where the criminal element has manifested itself, speaks volumes regarding [the] SAPS’s commitment to fighting crime. “This statement of the Board of Commissioners is fully supported by the Deputy National Commissioner: Corporate Services – Lieutenant-General Nobubele Mbekela, the Deputy National Commissioner: Policing – Lieutenant-General Kehla Sitole, and acting Divisional Commissioner Lieutenant-General Bongiwe Zulu. “Each and every individual provincial commissioner is fully behind this media statement and may be contacted by media representatives directly to verify this fact.”
